title: Drafting Proposal Responses

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposal responses covers the work of turning a request for proposal, a client brief, or an internal funding case into a structured written answer. In finance it usually means responding to requests from institutional clients, procurement teams, or investment committees, where the response must follow a fixed question set and cite the firm's own policies, past performance, and controls. The task sits between research, compliance review, and writing, and it is repetitive enough that agents can carry much of the first pass.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a document store holding prior responses, style guides, product and policy language, and approved figures, plus a retrieval layer that pulls the passages relevant to each question. A language model drafts against that retrieved material, and a workflow engine tracks which questions are answered, which are flagged, and which need a named human owner. Output usually lands in the firm's existing document tooling rather than a separate system, so reviewers work where they already work.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical run parses the request into its individual questions, matches each one to source material, and produces a draft answer with the supporting passage attached. Agents then check the draft against a rules list: no unapproved claims, no stale figures, no commitments the firm has not made before. A human reviewer edits, approves, or rejects each section, and the accepted text is written back into the response library so the next run has better material to draw on.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters more here than in most drafting work, because a response can become a contractual statement. Each answer should carry a link to the source it came from, a record of who approved it, and a note of when the underlying policy or figure was last confirmed. Firms also need a clear rule on what agents may never assert on their own, such as fees, guarantees, regulatory status, or performance claims, and a review step that catches anything the model produced without a source.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter integration with the systems that hold the truth, so drafts are assembled from live policy and product data rather than from a snapshot of old responses. Reviewers are likely to shift from writing first drafts to auditing them, which changes what skills the role rewards. The open questions are how much of a response can be approved without a person reading it, and how firms evidence that the answer they sent was accurate at the time it was sent.
